items.title: Casual legal: Restrictive covenants vs redevelopment (Alberta Municipalities); CBC News, Judge overrules century-old legal covenant, Feb 18, 2026

citations.finding: The Carruthers Caveat, registered as instrument 4387AI against Plan 2803AF lots, prohibits erecting any building other than a private dwelling house and limits development; in 2357596 Alberta Ltd v Antoniuk, 2026 ABKB 81 (February 2026) the Court of King's Bench discharged it from two Glenora lots (zoned medium-rise apartment in 2022), finding conflict with the zoning bylaw and public interest; the decision is fact-specific and under appeal. The caveat remains on more than 400 Glenora properties.
citations.establishes: That the 1911 covenant is a real registered instrument with dwelling-type restrictions still on title in 2026, as described by a municipal legal newsletter and reported by CBC; a court filing or judgment summary, not the covenant text.

items.title: Henderson's Edmonton City Directory (1926)
items.publisher: Henderson Directories (digitized by Internet Archive / University of Alberta Peel collection)

citations.finding: A Henderson's Edmonton City Directory for 1926 exists and is digitized (publisher Henderson Directories, date 1926). Its OCR text contains a 'Street Directory' section and hundreds of householder entries of the form 'h [house number] [street]', e.g. 'Ambler Mrs Eliza E h 11432 87th St', 'Allyn Frank L brklyr h 11236 126th St'. OCR quality is poor, so counts by neighbourhood could not be made reliably.
citations.establishes: That dwellings at specific residential street addresses in Edmonton were occupied in 1926; a directory-type record of the kind the brief accepts as occupancy evidence.

items.title: 1926 Census of the Prairie Provinces

citations.finding: Edmonton possessed established residential neighbourhoods with dwelling houses prior to and during 1926, though specific architectural classifications like 'single-detached' were not explicitly categorized in the 1926 Census schedules.
citations.establishes: The existence of built dwelling houses in Edmonton in 1926, although it does not provide the density threshold required by the brief.

items.title: History of Zoning in Edmonton

citations.finding: Edmonton's first comprehensive zoning bylaw was Bylaw 26-1933, which established one-family residential development zones. This leaves a gap from 1926 to 1933.
citations.establishes: The start date of Edmonton's first zoning bylaw (1933) and its focus on one-family residential zones.

items.title: 2001 Federal Census neighbourhood housing profiles: Glenora, Highlands, Westmount, Strathcona

citations.finding: 2001 federal census neighbourhood profiles (City of Edmonton tabulation) give occupied private dwellings by period of construction 'Before 1946': Glenora 260 of 1,495 (17.4%); Highlands 385 of 1,230 (31.3%); Westmount 785 of 3,070 (25.6%); Strathcona 770 of 5,150 (15.0%). Figures rounded for privacy.
citations.establishes: A lower bound on pre-1946 dwellings still occupied in 2001 in four neighbourhoods inside the 1917 boundary; does not isolate 1926 and does not give a net residential land area.

items.title: Zoning Bylaw Map - History, Edmonton Open Data Portal

citations.finding: The City's open-data 'Zoning Bylaw Map - History' dataset retains zoning polygons only from May 10, 2019 onward (weekly extracts), so no digitized 1933, 1961 or 1980 district map is available online for neighbourhood-level coverage calculation.
citations.establishes: Why the brief's exact coverage counts and shares for E1 to E5 could not be produced from public digital data.

items.title: History of Zoning in Edmonton (Attachment 1 to Zoning Bylaw Renewal Report #1, CR_6664)

citations.finding: Zoning Bylaw 26, enacted October 10, 1933, divided the city into 11 districts (A to K) including 'One-family Dwelling District, Two-family Dwelling District and Three and Six Storey Multiple Dwelling Districts'. 'The Bylaw largely favoured low-density development of single-family homes, with a majority of the lots in the city zoned One-Family Unit District.' Height limit in the B district 35 feet; side setback 10% of site width; accessory offices and businesses permitted in B. Figure 1 reproduces the 1933 district map.
citations.establishes: The existence, date, district structure and one-family emphasis of the first city-wide zoning instrument, and the City's characterization that most lots were zoned one-family; it is a secondary description of the bylaw text, and the minimum lot area for the B district is not stated.
citations.quote: The Bylaw largely favoured low-density development of single-family homes, with a majority of the lots in the city zoned One-Family Unit District.

citations.finding: The 1933 B One-Family Dwelling District also permitted accessory offices and business uses, 'making it a more mixed-use zone than the corresponding residential zones in Zoning Bylaw 12800', and the 1980 bylaw introduced Direct Control districts and statutory plan overlays that altered standard rules area by area.
citations.establishes: That era labels do not map onto today's meaning of a low-density residential zone and that coverage by a standard district was not uniform after 1980.

items.title: Historic Resources: Register and Inventory

citations.finding: The City's register lists numerous Edmonton residences built before 1926 and says designated Municipal Historic Resources are protected from demolition and must be maintained.
citations.establishes: Corroborates the survival of many pre-1926 residential buildings into the current period. The register does not establish current occupation, continuous use, or historical density.

items.title: Resources for Researching Your Building

citations.finding: The City warns that Henderson directories may omit occupants and explains that the Archives holds 1925 fire-insurance maps showing buildings, lots and materials. The webpage does not provide a completed 1926 dwelling-and-area dataset.
citations.establishes: The available occupation source has known omissions, while the map evidence needed for the brief's calculation requires archival reconstruction.
citations.quote: Henderson's may not list every occupant, spouse, occupation or ownership status.

items.title: Edmonton's Developing and Planned Neighbourhoods: Low Density Residential Lot Registrations

citations.finding: The City's 2014 report counted 83 planned or developing neighbourhoods in approved Area Structure Plans, including 73 with approved Neighbourhood Structure Plans. It reported low-density completion by NSP, with 40 neighbourhoods under development and 33 already 95 to 100 percent complete for low-density residential lots.
citations.establishes: Strong evidence that officially termed low-density housing was deliberately incorporated into dozens of Edmonton neighbourhood plans. It supports the cumulative count reading at cutoffs 5 and 10, but its form-based definition does not satisfy the brief's permitted-density rule.
citations.quote: A total of eighty three neighbourhoods (planned and developing) are in approved Area Structure Plans.

citations.finding: The same report estimated 91,516 potential single- or semi-detached low-density lots in approved plans as of December 2014: 43,518 in developing areas, 47,829 in planned areas and 169 in areas at least 95 percent complete.
citations.establishes: Scale far beyond isolated examples and documented planning intent through approved ASPs and NSPs. It does not provide each neighbourhood's covered-area share.

citations.finding: The 2014 report defines low-density development as single- and semi-detached lots rather than by permitted dwellings per hectare and does not count secondary suites, garden suites, row housing or small apartments.
citations.establishes: Its 73-NSP count cannot directly supply the brief's cross-era permitted-density classification.

items.title: Starling Neighbourhood Structure Plan

citations.finding: Starling's plan designates 46.23 hectares as Low Density Residential 1 at about 25 units per hectare, mostly single- and semi-detached housing, out of 58.4 residential hectares. That is 79.2 percent of residential land by reviewer arithmetic.
citations.establishes: One direct example exceeding the 50 percent coverage rule using residential land as denominator, with an identified density and housing forms. A plan establishes intent, not built outcome.

items.title: Inglewood Neighbourhood Profile

citations.finding: The Inglewood profile says the area was inside Edmonton by 1920 and developed as a low-density residential neighbourhood until the 1950s.
citations.establishes: Official historical characterization of an Edmonton area as low-density during the relevant early period. It does not report occupied dwellings, land area, denominator type, or dwellings per hectare for 1926.

citations.finding: The Inglewood profile says low-density units became a small proportion of that neighbourhood's units by the 2000s as apartment development increased.
citations.establishes: Shows that one early low-density example changed substantially, so its early classification cannot establish city-wide continuity by itself.

items.title: Net Residential Density Annual Report 2023, Redeveloping and Developing Areas
items.publisher: City of Edmonton, Urban Planning and Economy

citations.finding: The City's 2023 Net Residential Density Report defines low density residential (LDR) as 'single and semi-detached units', reports the redeveloping area (inside Anthony Henday Drive, which encloses all 1926 neighbourhoods) at 32 du/nrha overall in 2023, and maps planned densities in classes 'less than 30', '30 and 45' and 'greater than 45' du/nrha.
citations.establishes: The T2 threshold and denominator definition, and that LDR forms remain a large part of the 2023 stock (built outcome at the end of the window).
citations.quote: Net residential land area excludes rural residential parcels as well as parcels with non-residential land uses such as open spaces, road right-of-ways, commercial and institutional uses and undeveloped land.

citations.finding: As of December 2023, 86 residential neighbourhoods in the developing area were in the developing stage; 71 had NASPs or NSPs in effect, 48 of them approved in or before 2010; 'Older NSPs typically have lower planned residential densities, while more recent NSPs have planned densities greater than 35 du/nrha'; 'Most dwellings in this area continue to be LDR'. EMRB greenfield targets of 45 du/nrha took effect in 2017 for areas without approved plans.
citations.establishes: A count of neighbourhood-level statutory plans in effect at the end of the window (denominator 2 material) and that LDR is the dominant planned and built form in the developing area; it does not give each plan's LDR land share.

items.title: Edmonton Land Use Bylaw 5996, office consolidation version 7 (August 24, 1998), s. 110

citations.finding: Land Use Bylaw 5996 RF1 Single Detached Residential District (1998 consolidation): purpose 'To establish a District primarily for Single Detached Housing'; permitted uses Single Detached Housing, Limited Group Homes, Minor Home Occupations; Semi-detached, Duplex and Secondary Suites discretionary only where the side lot line abuts an industrial, commercial, row housing or apartment district; 'the minimum site area shall be 360 m2 (3,875.0 sq. ft.) per Dwelling'; minimum site width 12 m; maximum height 10 m; total site coverage 40%; 'a maximum of one Dwelling per lot shall be allowed' except where semi-detached, duplex or suites are allowed.
citations.establishes: E4 permitted forms and dimensional rules: 27.8 du/ha of site area maximum, one dwelling per lot as the norm (consolidation read, not the 1980 text as adopted).
citations.quote: the minimum site area shall be 360 m2 (3,875.0 sq. ft.) per Dwelling

items.title: Highlands Edmonton Historical Walking Tour, Centennial Edition 1912-2012
items.publisher: City of Edmonton (Heritage) with Highlands Historical Society

citations.finding: Highlands (subdivision plan filed June 1911, annexed December 1911): lots marketed from 1910 with a $2,500 minimum house cost; the developers built 24 houses on speculation in November 1912, doubling the house count on a 516-lot subdivision; named houses were built and occupied in 1912-1921 (Owen Residence 1912, Bell Residence 1912, occupied by the Bell family from 1921); by the 1920s some houses were 'divided into suites, and many were rented out'. House types described are two-storey wood-frame Foursquare houses.
citations.establishes: Documented built and occupied detached houses in Highlands before and through the 1920s, and their form; also that build-out was sparse (516 lots, roughly 48 houses by 1913).
citations.quote: The number of houses was doubled, but since it had 516 lots, The Highlands was still sparsely developed.

citations.finding: Early housing was not uniformly single-unit: by the 1920s Highlands houses were 'divided into suites, and many were rented out'; the 1913 Gibbard Block was an apartment building at the Highlands' edge. A 1926 household count would exceed the house count in such areas.
citations.establishes: That 'low density' cannot be equated with one household per building in 1926; a density figure would need dwelling units, not houses.

citations.finding: Highlands: announced August 1910 on land east of the city limits, subdivision plan filed June 1911, annexed December 1911; 516 lots; $2,500 minimum house cost; 'Unlike Glenora ... The Highlands was not regulated by legal restrictions. Instead, development was controlled by having buyers take out building permits before purchasing land'; laid out 'almost entirely ... in a grid pattern'.
citations.establishes: A third pre-1926 subdivision deliberately planned for high-value detached houses by developer control rather than covenant (evidence class: developer plans and lot layout).

citations.finding: For 1926-1933 the record accessed documents deliberate low-density planning in only three subdivisions (Glenora, Groat Estate/Westmount, Highlands). Highlands was explicitly 'not regulated by legal restrictions'. This is below both count cutoffs (5 and 10) for E0, and the share of then-existing neighbourhoods is unknown.
citations.establishes: That pre-zoning planning intent is documented for a handful of elite subdivisions, not 'many' neighbourhoods, on the evidence found.

items.title: Redeveloping/Developing Area Net Residential Density Report, 2021 Annual Report

citations.finding: The 2021 density report defines net residential land as excluding open space and road rights-of-way and reports a density band at or below 25 dwellings per net residential hectare. It contains no equivalent 1926 calculation.
citations.establishes: Provides a sourced modern threshold candidate and denominator definition, but not measurements that can classify a 1926 area without mixing denominators or eras.

citations.finding: The 2021 report identified 70 developing neighbourhoods, 55 with NSPs approved before 2010, and published planned net-residential densities by neighbourhood. Twelve listed neighbourhoods had planned density at or below 25 dwellings per net residential hectare by reviewer count.
citations.establishes: A direct Edmonton count above the primary cutoff of 10 under a broad variant using whole-neighbourhood planned density and the report's at-or-below-25 band. Overall planned density is not the brief's required permitted maximum or a covered-area measure.

citations.finding: The 2021 report says recent NSPs generally exceed 35 dwellings per net residential hectare and contain a more balanced range of dwelling types, while older NSPs typically have lower planned densities.
citations.establishes: Affirmatively cautions against treating every Edmonton neighbourhood plan as low-density or assuming a constant planning model across eras.

items.title: Griffith Residence Statement of Significance

citations.finding: The City's statement says the Griffith Residence was occupied from 1924 to 1928 and that Westmount had a large collection of single-detached homes built between 1911 and 1925.
citations.establishes: A second occupied residence at the exact cutoff and evidence that this was not an isolated housing form. It supplies neither dwelling count nor land area for the Westmount collection.

items.title: Hardisty Residence Statement of Historic Significance

citations.finding: The City states that the Hardisty Residence was occupied by George Smiley from 1925 to 1928. It was therefore occupied on 1926-09-02 and during calendar year 1926. The City designated the building as a Municipal Historic Resource in March 2025.
citations.establishes: Direct evidence of an occupied detached residence in Edmonton at the exact 1926 cutoff, plus evidence that the building remained extant in 2025. It does not provide lot area, a density calculation, or continuous residential use through 2026-09-02.

items.title: Resource Guide - Historical Land Use Bylaws

citations.finding: The City's historical resource guide identifies the principal regulatory sequence but also records incomplete map holdings, including only the east side of the 1961 and 1971 maps and only portions of some 1980s maps.
citations.establishes: The public inventory itself identifies gaps that prevent a complete era-by-era geographic overlay from the consulted online record.

items.title: Resource Guide: Historical Land Use Bylaws 1933-Present, version 1.5 (revised Aug 15, 2024)
items.publisher: City of Edmonton, Edmonton Tower Resource Centre

citations.finding: The Edmonton Tower Resource Centre lists the primary instruments and maps: 'The zoning bylaw of the City of Edmonton, no. 26 [October 10, 1933]' and its 1942 office consolidation; 'District map to accompany zoning bylaw no. 26 [October 10, 1933]'; Interim Development By-law 1339 [July 18, 1950]; Interim development by-law no. 2: bylaw no. 1988 [September 1, 1959]; zoning bylaw no. 2135 [as amended March 9, 1964] with zoning maps 1961-62; development control bylaws 2624 and 4949; Land Use Bylaw 5996 consolidations from July 3, 1980; Zoning Bylaw 12800 effective June 14, 2001.
citations.establishes: The catalogue of instruments and their dates, including that a 1933 district map exists; confirms the 1933 bylaw is no. 26 and shows the numbering discrepancy for the 1959 interim bylaw (1988 here, 1998 in the City history report).

items.title: Glenora - Edmonton Historical Board (with Old Glenora Conservation Association, Establishing the Association)
items.publisher: Edmonton Historical Board; Old Glenora Conservation Association (https://oldglenora.ca/establishing-the-association/)

citations.finding: Glenora and Groat Estate (Westmount): James Carruthers, who bought Malcolm Groat's property in 1906, registered restrictive covenants requiring that 'the houses to be erected on the said land shall be either detached or semi-detached' with minimum construction costs of $3,500 to $5,000 depending on location, and prohibiting commercial and religious buildings; the Glenora street layout followed the ravine topography in the Garden City manner. The Old Glenora Conservation Association describes the 1911 caveat as stipulating 'no commercial development, one dwelling per lot and established building setbacks' over land from Stony Plain Road to the river and from Groat Ravine to 142 Street.
citations.establishes: Documented deliberate pre-1926 planning of two subdivisions around detached or semi-detached houses by restrictive covenant (a non-public instrument class); the exact covenant text was not read.
citations.quote: the houses to be erected on the said land shall be either detached or semi-detached

items.title: Westmount - Edmonton Historical Board

citations.finding: Westmount / Groat Estate: 'The majority of homes were erected during the 1912 land boom'; residences ranged from brick or arts-and-crafts manors in Groat Estate to 'large clapboard homes' for young professionals; streetcar reached 142 Street by 1910.
citations.establishes: Built detached housing in Westmount before 1926 (form and period), not a dwelling count.

items.title: Edmonton annexations

citations.finding: City boundary history: Strathcona (Dec 20, 1911 / Feb 1, 1912), North Edmonton (July 1912), further 1912-1914 annexations, Village of West Edmonton/Calder (April 1917); 'No annexations occurred between 1917 and 1947' apart from small separations in 1921 and 1922; city area about 106 km2 in 1917, 221.6 km2 by 1964, 700.6 km2 after January 1, 1982.
citations.establishes: The boundary in force per era (secondary compilation; the City Archives' 1959 'History of Annexations' map, EAM-529, is the primary source and was identified but not read).

items.title: Glenora, Edmonton (with Highlands, Edmonton and Westmount, Edmonton)
items.publisher: Wikipedia, citing City of Edmonton municipal census

citations.finding: Glenora: Carruthers acquired the land in 1905-06; the Carruthers bridge (1910) opened development; the 1913 crash slowed it; The Graenon mansion dates to 1914; 'Three out of four residences are single-family dwellings' (2012 municipal census, 1,546 dwellings, 1.63 km2 gross area). Highlands: 1.15 km2 gross area; 90% single-family dwellings (2012). Westmount: 1.86 km2; 42% single-family, 54% apartments (2005).
citations.establishes: Gross neighbourhood areas and present-day housing mix (secondary compilation of City census data); used only for the non-classifying bounding figures below.

items.title: List of neighbourhoods in Edmonton

citations.finding: Edmonton has 375 developed neighbourhoods in 7 sectors (not counting planned but undeveloped ones); the central core comprises Downtown and 11 surrounding neighbourhoods.
citations.establishes: A present-day denominator (375) for the share reading; the then-existing denominators per era were not computed.

items.title: Edmonton Zoning Bylaw 12800, version 01.06.18, effective June 14, 2001, s. 110

citations.finding: Zoning Bylaw 12800 as adopted (effective June 14, 2001) s. 110 RF1: 'The purpose of this Zone is to provide primarily for Single Detached Housing'; permitted Single Detached Housing; Semi-detached, Duplex and Secondary Suites discretionary only on lots abutting industrial, commercial, row housing or apartment zones; minimum site area 360 m2 per dwelling; minimum site width 12.0 m; height 10.0 m; one dwelling per lot except where those forms are allowed.
citations.establishes: E5 initial permitted forms and dimensions (27.8 du/ha of site area).

items.title: J. David Hulchanski, The Origins of Urban Land Use Planning in Alberta, 1900-1945 (Research Paper No. 119, Centre for Urban and Community Studies, University of Toronto, January 1981), p. 23

citations.finding: Between 1918 and 1920 Edmonton took possession of some 70,000 lots through tax-arrears forfeiture after the 1913 collapse; the 1912 boom had subdivided far more land than was ever built on. Much of the 'residential' land inside the 1917 boundary in 1926 was vacant subdivided lots, not occupied housing.
citations.establishes: That built housing in 1926 was sparse relative to subdivided land; a registered plan alone did not mean occupation, which is why occupancy records matter for this claim.
citations.quote: Between 1918 and 1920 Edmonton took possession of some 70,000 lots

citations.finding: Before zoning: Bylaw 35 (1923) 'prescribed the space to be left vacant around buildings', 'limited the number and nature of buildings to be erected on a lot within certain parts of the city and declared certain streets or portions of streets to be purely residential'; clause 8 barred shops, stores, laundries, stables and any business use on lots abutting a residential street. Bylaw 30 (1925) confined noxious uses to specific areas. Not until the 1929 Town Planning Act could municipalities adopt comprehensive zoning; Edmonton's Town Planning Commission was created in August 1929 and directed to prepare a major street plan and a zoning bylaw rather than a master plan. Between 1933 and 1945 Bylaw 26 was amended 27 times.
citations.establishes: That partial residential-protection instruments existed in 1926 (E0) and that comprehensive zoning began only in 1933; a units-per-lot limit existed in 'certain parts of the city' under Bylaw 35, but its geography is not given.
citations.quote: It limited the number and nature of buildings to be erected on a lot within certain parts of the city and declared certain streets or portions of streets to be purely residential.

citations.finding: Dale (quoted by Hulchanski) argued the 1933 bylaw 'completely failed to achieve or promote rational land use. It merely attempted to separate particular use-districts'; there was no master plan, amendments were approved 'on most any grounds', and the bylaw 'achieved what they were actually intended to achieve -- protection of certain districts, mainly better quality residential areas, from undesirable uses'. Hulchanski also records Edmonton took possession of some 70,000 tax-forfeited lots in 1918-1920.
citations.establishes: That the 1933 one-family districting was use-separation applied largely to vacant subdivided land rather than neighbourhood design, which bears on whether 'zoned one-family' equals 'planned around low-density housing' and on which denominator (planned versus occupied) applies.
citations.quote: It merely attempted to separate particular use-districts and as such was rather more regulative and negative than either constructive or positive.

items.title: City of Edmonton Population, Historical (updated August 2008)

citations.finding: Edmonton's population in 1926 was 65,163 (City of Edmonton historical population table, compiled from census tabulations); 1921: 58,821; 1931: 79,059. The same table lists annexations of Strathcona (Feb 1, 1912), North Edmonton (July 18, 1912) and Calder (April 26, 1917) with the next annexation Beverly (Dec 30, 1961), so the 1917 boundary was the boundary in force in 1926.
citations.establishes: City population in 1926 and the annexation sequence fixing the 1926 boundary at the 1917 limits.

items.title: Ellerslie Neighbourhood Structure Plan, Office Consolidation June 2023

citations.finding: Ellerslie Neighbourhood Structure Plan (Bylaw 12581, approved May 1, 2001; consolidated June 2023): 'Residential densities of 25 units per net residential hectare for low density residential and 50 units per hectare for medium density residential'; within the LDR area 'housing forms will be predominantly single and semi-detached housing'; plan area 155.18 ha.
citations.establishes: The T1 threshold and an example of a statutory plan that designates LDR land at 25 du/nrha (planning intent, not outcome).
citations.quote: Residential densities of 25 units per net residential hectare for low density residential and 50 units per hectare for medium density residential

items.title: Highlands Neighbourhood Planning Study, Office Consolidation June 2021

citations.finding: The Highlands Neighbourhood Planning Study (approved by Council March 12, 1985; repealed by Bylaw 19725, June 8, 2021) described Highlands as 'predominantly a low density residential community' and tabulated 1983 dwellings: 1,023 single family (81.5%), 128 single family containing a suite (10.2%), 18 semi-detached/duplex, 29 multi-family, 57 apartment units.
citations.establishes: A neighbourhood-specific plan in E4 that planned around low-density housing and recorded the built mix (outcome) separately, including one in ten houses containing a suite.

items.title: Edmonton Zoning Bylaw 12800, s. 110 (RF1) Single Detached Residential Zone, web consolidation
items.source_date: amendments dated 2007 to 2021; consolidation as archived

citations.finding: Zoning Bylaw 12800 RF1 as last amended: purpose 'to provide for Single Detached Housing while allowing other forms of small scale housing in the form of Secondary Suites, Garden Suites, Semi-detached Housing and Duplex Housing' (Charter Bylaw 18638, December 10, 2018); Secondary Suites and Garden Suites permitted; minimum site area for Single Detached Housing 250.8 m2, minimum site width 7.5 m (Bylaw 18050, June 12, 2017); Duplex 300 m2 and 10.0 m; Semi-detached 488.4 m2 and 14.8 m; height 10.0 m; site coverage 40-42%.
citations.establishes: That the RF1 label's permissions changed within E5: by 2018 a detached house plus secondary suite plus garden suite on a 250.8 m2 lot was permitted (39.9 du/ha principal only; 119.6 du/ha all dwellings).

citations.finding: Under T1 (25 du/nrha) the RF1 instruments of 1980-2001 (360 m2 per dwelling, 27.8 du/ha) are not low density by permitted density, and the 2015-2023 RF1 (250.8 m2, suites permitted) and the 2024 RS zone (75 m2 per dwelling, up to 8 dwellings) exceed both thresholds. The 'low density' label attached to RF1 in City documents therefore does not survive the brief's predeclared measure under T1, and the city-wide instrument in force at the end of the window does not plan around low-density housing under either threshold.
citations.establishes: That instrument classification depends on the threshold chosen and that E6 fails the low-density test on the zoning-instrument variant.

items.title: Canada Year Book appendix: Census of the Prairie Provinces in 1926 (p. 1034)
items.publisher: Dominion Bureau of Statistics / Statistics Canada

citations.finding: The 1926 Census of the Prairie Provinces was taken 'as of date June 1, 1926' under the Statistics Act of 1918; the page consulted gives provincial and Manitoba figures, not the Edmonton city figure.
citations.establishes: Date and legal basis of the 1926 census; corroborates that a 1926 enumeration exists as a potential occupancy record.
citations.quote: A census of the Prairie Provinces was, therefore, taken as of date June 1, 1926

items.title: Zoning Bylaw 20001 Amendments

citations.finding: The current amendment page showed Bylaw 21474 effective August 1, 2026 and amendments through July 6, 2026 when accessed on September 1. It cannot establish which consolidation will govern on September 2.
citations.establishes: The consolidation available one day before the fixed endpoint cannot conclusively establish the endpoint version.

items.title: Zoning Bylaw 20001, Section 2.10 RS - Small Scale Residential Zone

citations.finding: The current RS Small Scale Residential Zone allows detached, attached and multi-unit housing, up to eight dwellings on an interior site, with a minimum 75 square metres of site area per dwelling and 45 percent site coverage. This computes to 133.3 permitted dwellings per site hectare.
citations.establishes: The main current small-scale zone is not low-density under a 25-dwelling-per-hectare threshold when classified by maximum permitted site density. This challenges an unqualified end-of-window verdict.
citations.quote: The maximum number of Dwellings on an Interior Site is 8.

items.title: 2.10 RS - Small Scale Residential Zone, Zoning Bylaw 20001
items.source_date: consolidation viewed 2026-09-02; latest amendment visible Bylaw 21474

citations.finding: Continuity to the end of the window: the zone in force on 2026-09-02 under Charter Bylaw 20001 (passed October 23, 2023, effective January 1, 2024, online consolidation 'for convenience only') is the RS Small Scale Residential Zone, whose purpose is 'To allow for a range of small scale Residential development up to 3 Storeys in Height, including detached, attached, and multi-unit Residential housing'. Detached houses remain a permitted form.
citations.establishes: That single detached housing remained a permitted use in the principal residential zone at the end of the window (legal permission, not built stock).

citations.finding: Charter Bylaw 20001 RS zone: 'The maximum number of Dwellings on an Interior Site is 8' (s. 3.2.1); minimum site area per dwelling 75.0 m2 (4.1.1); minimum site width 7.5 m (4.1.3); minimum site depth 30.0 m; permitted forms include single detached, semi-detached, duplex, row housing, cluster housing and small apartments; height 9.5 m; site coverage 45% (47% in specified conditions).
citations.establishes: E6 permitted density of 133.3 du/ha of site area, above both thresholds; the instrument in force at the end of the window.
citations.quote: The maximum number of Dwellings on an Interior Site is 8
